facts.fact: The 1st Tirthankara is Rishabhanatha (Adinath), whose symbol is the Bull.
Rishabhanatha, the 1st Tirthankara, was born at Ayodhya.
The 2nd Tirthankara is Ajitanatha, whose symbol is the Elephant.
Ajitanatha, the 2nd Tirthankara, was born at Ayodhya.
The 3rd Tirthankara is Sambhavanatha, whose symbol is the Horse.
Sambhavanatha, the 3rd Tirthankara, was born at Sravasti.
The 4th Tirthankara is Abhinandananatha, whose symbol is the Ape.
Abhinandananatha, the 4th Tirthankara, was born at Ayodhya.
The 5th Tirthankara is Sumatinatha, whose symbol is the Heron.
Sumatinatha, the 5th Tirthankara, was born at Ayodhya.
The 6th Tirthankara is Padmaprabha, whose symbol is the Lotus.
Padmaprabha, the 6th Tirthankara, was born at Kausambi.
The 7th Tirthankara is Suparshvanatha, whose symbol is the Swastika.
Suparshvanatha, the 7th Tirthankara, was born at Varanasi.
The 8th Tirthankara is Chandraprabha, whose symbol is the Moon.
Chandraprabha, the 8th Tirthankara, was born at Chandrapuri.
The 9th Tirthankara is Suvidhinatha (Pushpadanta), whose symbol is the Dolphin (sea dragon).
Suvidhinatha, the 9th Tirthankara, was born at Kakandi.
The 10th Tirthankara is Shitalanatha, whose symbol is the Shrivatsa.
Shitalanatha, the 10th Tirthankara, was born at Bhadrikapuri.
The 11th Tirthankara is Shreyansanatha, whose symbol is the Rhinoceros.
Shreyansanatha, the 11th Tirthankara, was born at Simhapuri.
The 12th Tirthankara is Vasupujya, whose symbol is the Buffalo.
Vasupujya, the 12th Tirthankara, was born at Champapuri.
The 13th Tirthankara is Vimalanatha, whose symbol is the Boar.
Vimalanatha, the 13th Tirthankara, was born at Kampilya.
The 14th Tirthankara is Anantanatha, whose symbol is the Hawk (or Bear).
Anantanatha, the 14th Tirthankara, was born at Ayodhya.
The 15th Tirthankara is Dharmanatha, whose symbol is the Thunderbolt.
Dharmanatha, the 15th Tirthankara, was born at Ratnapuri.
The 16th Tirthankara is Shantinatha, whose symbol is the Deer.
Shantinatha, the 16th Tirthankara, was born at Hastinapur.
The 17th Tirthankara is Kunthunatha, whose symbol is the Goat.
Kunthunatha, the 17th Tirthankara, was born at Hastinapur.
The 18th Tirthankara is Aranatha, whose symbol is the Fish (or Nandyavarta).
Aranatha, the 18th Tirthankara, was born at Hastinapur.
The 19th Tirthankara is Mallinatha, whose symbol is the Water Pot.
Mallinatha, the 19th Tirthankara, was born at Mithila.
The 20th Tirthankara is Munisuvrata, whose symbol is the Tortoise.
Munisuvrata, the 20th Tirthankara, was born at Rajagriha.
The 21st Tirthankara is Naminatha, whose symbol is the Blue Lotus.
Naminatha, the 21st Tirthankara, was born at Mithila.
The 22nd Tirthankara is Neminatha (Arishtanemi), whose symbol is the Conch Shell.
Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara, was born at Sauripur.
The 23rd Tirthankara is Parshvanatha, whose symbol is the Snake.
Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara, was born at Varanasi.
The 24th Tirthankara is Mahavira, whose symbol is the Lion.
Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, was born at Kundagrama.
Jainism emerged in the 6th century BCE.
Jainism arose as a reaction against costly Vedic sacrifices, rituals and Brahmin dominance.
The Kshatriyas and Vaishyas opposed Brahmin domination and backed the new egalitarian faiths.
Jainism offered equality and relief from the Varna system.
Mahavira taught in Prakrit, the language of the common people, which helped Jainism spread.
Jainism attracted followers through its stress on Ahimsa (non-violence) and self-discipline.
Jainism recognises 24 Tirthankaras (ford-makers).
Tirthankara means a 'ford-maker' — a liberated teacher who shows the way across the ocean of rebirth.
Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara, is said to have founded the Ikshvaku dynasty.
Rishabhanatha (Adinath) was the first Tirthankara.
Vardhamana Mahavira was the 24th and last Tirthankara.
Mallinatha, the 19th Tirthankara, is the only female Tirthankara (Svetambara view).
Mahavira was born in 540 BCE.
Mahavira was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali in present-day Bihar.
Mahavira's father Siddhartha was head of the Jnatrika clan.
Mahavira's mother Trishala was a Lichchavi princess.
Mahavira married Yashoda (not Yashodhara, the Buddha's wife).
Mahavira had a daughter named Anojja (Priyadarshana).
Mahavira renounced worldly life at the age of 30.
Mahavira practised severe austerities for 12 years before enlightenment.
Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana (Kaivalya) at the age of 42.
Mahavira preached for 30 years, mainly in Kosala, Magadha and Mithila.
Mahavira died at the age of 72 in 468 BCE.
Mahavira attained nirvana (died) at Pavapuri (Pawapuri) in Bihar.
Jain tradition dates Mahavira to 599–527 BCE (historians often use 540–468 BCE).
Mahavira was called Jina, 'the conqueror'; his followers are called Jainas.
Mahavira was also called Nirgrantha ('free from bonds') and Kevalin (the omniscient).
Mahavira attained Kaivalya under a sal tree at Jrimbhikagrama on the bank of the river Rijupalika.
Mahavira's mother Trishala was the sister of Chetaka, the Lichchhavi chief of Vaishali.
Mahavira's elder brother was Nandivardhana.
Indrabhuti Gautama was the first of the eleven Ganadharas of Mahavira.
Jamali, Mahavira's son-in-law, led the first schism in the Jain order.
Makkhali Gosala, who lived with Mahavira for about six years, founded the Ajivika sect.
Mahavira preached in Ardhamagadhi, a Prakrit language.
Mahavira's father was named Siddhartha, the same as the Buddha's personal name; the Buddha's father was Suddhodana.
Parshvanatha was the 23rd Tirthankara and preached before Mahavira.
Parshvanatha taught four vows — non-violence, truth, non-stealing and non-possession.
Parshvanatha believed in the eternity of matter.
Parshvanatha was the son of King Ashvasena of Varanasi (Kashi).
Parshvanatha lived about 250 years before Mahavira (c. 8th century BCE) and is accepted as historical.
Parshvanatha attained nirvana at Sammed Shikhar (Parasnath hill).
The goal of Jainism is Moksha (Nirvana) — liberation from the cycle of birth and death by removing karma.
The five great vows are called the Pancha Mahavratas.
Ahimsa means non-violence towards all living beings.
Satya means always speaking the truth.
Asteya means not stealing — not taking what is not freely given.
Aparigraha means renouncing possessions — non-attachment.
Brahmacharya (celibacy) was the fifth vow, added by Mahavira to Parshvanatha's four.
Householders follow milder versions of the five vows called Anuvratas.
The Three Jewels (Ratnatraya/Triratna) of Jainism are Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct.
Samyak Darshan means Right Faith.
Samyak Gyan means Right Knowledge.
Samyak Charitra means Right Conduct.
Jiva is the conscious soul that accumulates karma.
Ajiva is non-living matter.
Jainism holds that every object, even the smallest particle, has a soul.
Jainism holds that karma is the bane of the soul and penance destroys karma.
Jainism rejects a creator God; it recognises gods but places them below the Jina.
Sallekhana is the Jain practice of voluntary fasting unto death.
Unlike Buddhism, Jainism did not sharply condemn the varna system, explaining birth by past karma.
Because farming harms insects, Ahimsa pushed Jains into trade and commerce.
Anekantavada holds that reality can be understood only from multiple perspectives.
Syadvada holds that all judgments are conditional.
In Syadvada, 'Syat' means 'maybe'.
Anekantavada teaches that absolute truth is beyond human comprehension.
Mati Jnana is knowledge through the senses and mind.
Sruta Jnana is knowledge from scriptures and teachings.
Avadhi Jnana is clairvoyant knowledge of distant objects or events.
Manahparyaya Jnana is telepathic knowledge of others' thoughts.
Kevala Jnana (omniscience) is the highest form of knowledge.
The Swastika symbolises the peace and well-being of all humans.
Nandavarta is a large swastika with nine endpoints, symbolising spiritual advancement.
Bhadrasana is a throne sanctified by the feet of the Tirthankaras.
Shrivatsa is a mark on the chest of Tirthankaras, representing the pure soul.
Darpana is a mirror, symbolising self-reflection.
Minayugala, a pair of fish, symbolises conquest over sexual desire.
Vardhamanaka, a shallow dish or lamp, stands for increase in wealth and merit.
Kalasha, a pot of pure water, stands for purity and the well-being of all beings.
Digambara means 'sky-clad' (monks practise nudity).
Svetambara means 'white-clad' (monks wear white).
Svetambaras hold that women can attain liberation; Digambaras hold that a woman must first be reborn as a man.
Digambara idols are nude with eyes downcast; Svetambara idols are adorned with eyes open.
Bhadrabahu led the migration to the south during the 12-year famine (Digambara tradition).
Sthulbhadra led the monks who stayed in Magadha (Svetambara tradition).
Sthanakavasi (a Svetambara sub-sect) pray to saints, not idols; their saints wear a muhapatti.
The Sthanakvasi sect belongs to Jainism (UPSC 2018).
Murtipujaka (Deravasi), a Svetambara sub-sect, worship idols in temples; their saints do not wear a muhapatti.
Terapanthi (Svetambara) pray to saints, not idols, and their saints wear a muhapatti.
The Mula Sangh (Digambara) is associated with Acharya Kundakunda and known from 430 AD.
Branches of the Mula Sangh include the Nandi, Sena, Deva and Simha Ganas.
The Bisapantha (Digambara) worship Tirthankaras, Yakshas and Yakshinis and accept Bhattarakas as dharma gurus.
The Digambar Terapantha use dry substitutes for flowers and fruits and reject Bhattarakas.
The Taranpantha refute idolatry and keep sacred books in their temples for worship.
The First Jain Council was held at Pataliputra in about 300 BCE.
The First Jain Council was presided over by Sthulbhadra.
The First Jain Council compiled the canon into 12 Angas.
The Second Jain Council was held at Vallabhi (Gujarat) in 512 CE.
The Second Jain Council was presided over by Devardhigani Kshemasarmana.
The Second Jain Council added the Upangas and made the final compilation of the scriptures.
Agam literature holds Mahavira's direct teachings, compiled by his followers.
The twelve Ang-agamas were compiled by the Ganadharas, Mahavira's immediate disciples.
The Ang-bahya-agamas (secondary texts) were written by Shrutakevalins, who knew at least ten Purvas.
The 12th Anga, Drastivad, contains the fourteen Purvas, the oldest sacred Jain texts.
All Agam literature is written in Prakrit (Ardhamagadhi).
Non-Agam Jain literature is written in many languages including Sanskrit, Kannada, Tamil, Gujarati and Hindi.
The Acharanga Sutra, the first Anga, lays down rules of conduct for monks.
The Bhagavati Sutra gives a list of the 16 Mahajanapadas.
The Kalpasutra, on the lives of the Tirthankaras, is ascribed to Bhadrabahu.
The Parishishtaparvan, a Jaina text, was written by Hemachandra.
The Trishashti-lakshana Mahapurana is a Jaina (Digambara) text.
Nettipakarana and Avadanashataka are Buddhist, not Jaina, texts.
Jain rock-cut caves where monks lived are called Layana or Gumphas.
The Jain caves at Ellora (Maharashtra) are Caves 30 onwards (30–35 in the source; 30–34 in most references).
Mangi-Tungi and Gajapantha are Jain caves in Maharashtra.
Udayagiri-Khandagiri and Hathi-gumpha are Jain caves in Odisha.
Sittanavasal is a Jain cave in Tamil Nadu, known for its paintings.
The Gomateshwara (Bahubali) monolith, one of the tallest in the world, is at Shravanabelagola, Karnataka.
The 108-ft Statue of Ahimsa (Rishabhanatha) stands on the Mangi-Tungi hills, Maharashtra.
The Dilwara temples at Mount Abu, Rajasthan, are renowned for intricate marble carving.
The Girnar and Palitana Jain temples are in Gujarat.
Muktagiri is a Jain temple site in Maharashtra.
Jain temples are called Jinalayas.
A Manastambha is an ornamental pillar with a Tirthankara image facing all four directions, in front of Jain temples.
Basadis are Jain monastic establishments or temples, prominent in Karnataka.
Mahavira had eleven disciples called Ganadharas (heads of schools).
Arya Sudharma, the only Ganadhara surviving Mahavira, became the first Thera of the Jain order.
Udayin, the successor of Ajatasatru, was a devoted Jaina.
Chandragupta Maurya, a Jain, migrated with Bhadrabahu to South India.
Mathura and Ujjain were major Jain centres in the early centuries CE.
The Theras Sambhutavijaya and Bhadrabahu led the Jain order in the Nanda period.
Kharavela of Kalinga, a Jain king, recorded his patronage in the Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri.
Chandragupta Maurya ended his life by Sallekhana on Chandragiri hill, Shravanabelagola.
Kumarapala, the Solanki (Chalukya) king of Gujarat, patronised Jainism under the guidance of Hemachandra.
Amoghavarsha I (Rashtrakuta), the Western Gangas and the Kadambas patronised Jainism in the Deccan and south.
Sammed Shikhar (Parasnath hill, Jharkhand) is where 20 of the 24 Tirthankaras attained nirvana.
The Gomateshwara statue was made c. 981 CE for Chamundaraya, minister of the Western Ganga king.
The Gomateshwara monolith is about 57 ft (17 m) tall and stands on Vindhyagiri hill.
The Mahamastakabhisheka of Gomateshwara is held every 12 years.
Dilwara's Vimal Vasahi temple was built in 1031 CE by Vimal Shah, minister of the Solanki king Bhima I.
Dilwara's Luna Vasahi temple was built by the brothers Vastupala and Tejapala.
The Ranakpur Adinath temple (Rajasthan) is famed for its 1,444 carved pillars.
Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat) is linked with the 22nd Tirthankara Neminatha.
Palitana lies on the Shatrunjaya hills, covered with hundreds of Jain temples.
Kankali Tila at Mathura yielded a Jain stupa and sculptures.
Sittanavasal (Pudukkottai) is famous for Jain cave paintings.
Danavulapadu in YSR Kadapa district (AP) is a Jain site with Rashtrakuta-period remains.
Ramatheertham (Vizianagaram, AP) has both Jain and Buddhist remains.
The Kolanupaka Jain temple is in Telangana, not Andhra Pradesh.
Anekantavada promotes intellectual and social tolerance today.
Aparigraha can help curb consumerism and greed.
Jain Ahimsa influenced Mahatma Gandhi (through Raychandbhai Mehta).
